How close the solver has to get before it stops, measured as the total change in flow from one trial to the next, divided by the total flow in the links. A smaller number is more exact and takes longer.

where: Settings dialog: apply to all field

The accuracy at which the solver begins taking smaller steps, which can help an oscillating network to converge. Zero means the solver never damps.

A single factor applied to every demand in the network at once. Each scenario can have its own, so average day, maximum day or peak hour can be created by changing only this setting.

The exponent in EPANET’s emitter equation for sprinklers and leaks: flow = coefficient x pressure raised to this exponent. It only changes the answer where a node has an emitter, which for now means a network read from an EPANET file.

Enable this to use the built-in solver where possible. Otherwise, the EPANET solver from the US EPA is always used. The built-in solver is not used for extended period simulations or active PRV, PSV, or FCV. The first time the EPANET solver is used, about 650 KB is downloaded and then kept on this device. Where a pipe carries a minor (local) loss, the two solvers disagree in the last digits: EPANET rounds the value it uses for gravity, so its minor losses come out very slightly lower than the exact form.
An additional test the solver must pass before it stops: the maximum change in any one pipe’s flow from one trial to the next. Zero means do not apply this test.
An additional test the solver must pass before it stops: the largest head error remaining in any one pipe. Zero means do not apply this test.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: add field
tip: Adds a row to the design table and opens it for editing.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: applies field
tip: Applies to: Comma separated list of ID prefixes for assets that use this property, such as J,L,R.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: design field
tip: One row per custom property, and each opens to show: Key, Label, Applies to, Validate as, Allow or restrict, the characters field named by that choice, Length lower limit, Length upper limit, Low limit, High limit.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: high field
tip: High limit: This is the largest value you expect. Numbers are compared as numbers and text in dictionary order.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: key field
tip: Key: A property is stored under this name. Spaces are not allowed, and a prefix is added for you so that your key can never collide with a built-in field.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: label field
tip: Label: A reader sees this on the properties box, in Find and at the head of a table column.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: length field
tip: Length upper limit: Any longer entry is flagged.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: low field
tip: Low limit: This is the smallest value you expect. Numbers are compared as numbers and text in dictionary order.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: minlength field
tip: Length lower limit: Any shorter entry is flagged, which is how you find the empty and the half-typed entries.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: remove field
tip: Removes this property from the design table. Values already typed on your assets are kept in the file and come back if you design the same key again.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: restrict mode field
tip: Allow or restrict: The given characters are either the only ones a value may use or the ones it may not use.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: restrict field
tip: Restrict these characters: A value may use only the characters listed here, or none of them, where "@" means any letter; "#" means any numeric digit, and you must separately list "-", ".", and "," if they are allowed; and any white space characters must be between other characters.

where: Settings > Custom properties design table: validate field
tip: Validate as: This says what a good value looks like. The case rules read the English alphabet only, which is a stated limit. Choose Do not validate to accept anything.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: basic field
tip: Checked, a scenario is simply the values you set in it. Unchecked, this menu also offers the Alternatives preview table, which shows how those values are grouped by category and invites your feedback.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: mark field
tip: The amber ring means this asset holds a value that belongs to the scenario {name} alone.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: override field
tip: Checked means this scenario has an entry for this value, even when it is the same number as Base. Clear the box to use the Base value again.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: overrides field
tip: Each of those values is marked on the map with an amber ring. Switch to {base} to see the drawing without them.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset average day field
tip: Demand multiplier 1: every demand as entered, which is taken to be average day demand.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset fire max day field
tip: Max day demand (multiplier 2.0). Run Fire flow analysis in this scenario: it adds the fire flow at each junction on top of this demand.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset flow max field
tip: Flow test calibration for a design network at the max flow reported. In this scenario, set the demand at the flowing junction to the max flow measured, and the demand at all other junctions to 0.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset flow mid field
tip: Flow test calibration for a design network at the first flow reported. In this scenario, set the demand at the flowing junction to the first flow measured, and the demand at all other junctions to 0.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset flow static field
tip: Flow test calibration for a design network at 0 flow. In this scenario, set the demand at all junctions to 0.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset max day field
tip: Demand multiplier 2.0 times average day, a placeholder value. Most systems fall between 1.2 and 3.0 (National Research Council, 2006). Set your own system's in Settings, Calculation, Hydraulics, Demand multiplier.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: preset peak hour field
tip: Demand multiplier 3.0 times average day, a placeholder value. Most systems fall between 3.0 and 6.0 (National Research Council, 2006). Set your own system's in Settings, Calculation, Hydraulics, Demand multiplier.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: push field
tip: Every scenario goes back to the Base value for the properties whose labels are showing right now. Values entered for them in any scenario are discarded.

where: Scenarios menu / Properties box: scenario field
tip: The set of values the drawing is showing and the page is solving right now. Click to switch scenarios, or to add, rename, or delete one.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: mixing fraction field
tip: The share of the tank volume that the inlet zone takes up, between 0 and 1. Only two-compartment mixing uses it. Blank means that the whole tank is the inlet zone.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: mixing model field
tip: How the water already in this tank mixes with the water coming in. Complete mixing stirs the whole tank at once. Two-compartment mixing fills an inlet zone first and passes the rest on. FIFO plug flow moves the water through in the order it arrived. LIFO plug flow stacks it, so the last water in is the first water out. The choice changes the water age and the residual, and it does not change any pressure or flow.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: chemical name field
tip: The chemical you are tracking, for example Chlorine. Leave it blank for EPANET's own default label, Chemical. Shown on your reports, but not used in the calculations.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: diffusivity field
tip: How readily the chemical spreads through water, relative to chlorine. Blank uses EPANET's own default of 1.0.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: initial field
tip: How much of the chemical this node holds when the run starts. A reservoir holds its own value for the whole run, which is how the residual leaving a treatment plant is usually stated. Blank means 0.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: mass units field
tip: The units half of the quality entry, EPANET's own two choices.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: tolerance field
tip: How much two adjoining parcels of water may differ in concentration before EPANET treats them as one. Blank uses EPANET's own default of 0.01.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: bulk field
tip: Reaction in the body of the water (see EPANET Help), used for every pipe and tank that does not carry its own. A negative number decays the chemical and a positive one increases it. Blank means no bulk reaction.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: limiting field
tip: A concentration the chemical moves toward instead of decaying to nothing or growing without end. The reaction slows as the water approaches it and stops there. Use consistent units. No limit if blank.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: order bulk field
tip: The exponent the concentration is raised to for reaction in the body of the water. Any real number is allowed. 1 is the default value and is used for most chlorine decay modelling. 0 makes the rate independent of how much chemical is there.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: order tank field
tip: The exponent the concentration is raised to for reaction in the water held in a tank, separate from the bulk reaction order so a tank can react on a different order from the pipes. Any real number is allowed, and 1 is the default. EPANET states it as ORDER TANK in a file and offers no box for it in its own interface.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: order wall field
tip: 1 means that the wall reaction is dependent on the concentration in the bulk flow. 0 means it is not.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: pipe field
tip: Reaction in the body of the water (see EPANET Help). A negative number decays the chemical and a positive one increases it. Blank means to use the coefficient set for the whole network under Settings, Calculation, Quality.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: rough corr field
tip: Correlates the wall reaction to each pipe’s own roughness, so a rougher pipe reacts faster. When it is set, a wall coefficient is worked out for each pipe from that pipe’s roughness, and the single wall coefficient above is no longer used. Not used if blank.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: tank field
tip: Reaction in the water held in this tank, as a rate in 1/day. A negative number decays the chemical and a positive one grows it. Water stands in a tank far longer than it stands in any pipe, so this is often where a residual is lost. Blank means to use the bulk reaction coefficient set for the whole network under Settings, Calculation, Quality.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: wall field
tip: Reaction at the pipe wall (see EPANET Help) used for every pipe with no entry. A negative number decays the chemical. Blank means no wall reaction.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: concentration field
tip: How much of the chemical is left at this point after it has travelled and reacted. The units are yours as labelled with the chemical name under Settings, Calculation, Quality.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: source share field
tip: How much of the water reaching this point came from the trace node. This is what the Source trace analysis reports.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: water age field
tip: How long the water reaching this point has been in the system. Where flows meet, the number is the average of the arriving ages, weighted by flow. In a tank it is the average age of the water held, so a tank that turns over slowly usually holds the oldest water in a network. There is no regulatory limit to compare it against, so judge the number against your own system.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: pattern field
tip: A time pattern that scales the dose through the run, for a feed that is not constant. No pattern means that the dose is the same at every step.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: quality field
tip: How strong the dose is. For every type but the mass booster this is a concentration, in the units named beside the chemical under Settings, Calculation, Quality; for a mass booster it is a mass flow per minute. Blank means no chemical source, functionally equivalent to 0.

where: Settings > Calculation > Quality or Properties box: type field
tip: What kind of chemical source dosing is applied here based on the Source Quality value? Concentration source uses the value as a concentration applied to the external inflow (reservoir or negative demand). Mass booster adds a fixed mass flow per minute to that entering the node from other points in the network. Setpoint booster ensures that the concentration leaving the node is no lower than the value. Flow-paced booster source adds a fixed concentration to that resulting from the mixing of all inflow to the node from other points in the network

where: Reports dialogs: col mean err field
tip: The mean of the absolute differences between each observed value and the computed value at the same time.
Number of observations: the measurements at this location that were compared.

where: Reports dialogs: col rms err field
tip: Root mean square error: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between observed and computed values.

A text file with a location ID, a time, and a measured value on each line. The time is measured from the start of the simulation, in decimal hours or hours:minutes. A semicolon starts a comment. A line with only a time and a value belongs to the location above it.
The quantity the calibration file measures. One file is held for each parameter.

where: Reports dialogs: col avg kw field
tip: The average power used when this pump was running. It is not averaged over idle periods so that a pump that was idle for much of the extended period simulation still reports the power it used while it ran.
Whatever you write here is printed beside every money figure. It is only a label, but be consistent.
What the utility charges per kW for the peak load demanded by the pumps in the system.
The wire-to-water efficiency used for every pump that does not carry an efficiency curve of its own. EPANET uses 75 percent when nothing is stated.
A pattern that multiplies the price at each pattern step, which is how an off-peak rate is specified. Leave it empty for constant price throughout the run.
What one kilowatt hour costs. It applies to every pump that does not carry a price of its own. Blank means 0.
What one kilowatt hour costs at this pump. Blank means to use the price set for the whole network under Settings, Energy.
Compare measured field data from a calibration file with the last run: statistics, a correlation plot, and mean comparisons.
Every node and every link at every reporting time step of the last run, as one table you can download or print.
What changed over the last extended period simulation, in time order: pumps and valves opening or closing, tanks filling, emptying, filling up or running dry, and steps that did not fully converge.
What the EPANET solver itself printed about the last run: whether it converged, and anything it warned about. It is the solver’s own text, not ours.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve library link field
tip: Opens the Libraries box on its Curves section, where a curve is added, described, edited and deleted. An asset states which curve it uses.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: fittings field
tip: A list of fittings from the project library. Its quantities and coefficients are added up into this pipe’s minor loss coefficient, and the coefficient box is then read only. Leave this unselected to type the coefficient yourself.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pipetype field
tip: The pipe type in the project library that this pipe uses. Properties included in the pipe type are disabled for editing here. Detach the pipe type to enable editing here.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: gpv curve source field
tip: The curve in the Libraries box that says how much head this valve loses at each flow. Several valves can use the same curve, and editing it there changes all of them.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: control field
tip: A one-line rule using EPANET syntax. Use consistent project units. Keywords must be in English. Examples: LINK 12 CLOSED IF NODE 23 ABOVE 20 (Link 12 will be closed when the level in Tank 23 exceeds 20 ft); LINK 12 OPEN IF NODE 130 BELOW 30 (Link 12 will be opened if the pressure at Node 130 drops below 30 psi); LINK PUMP02 1.5 AT TIME 16 (The relative speed of pump PUMP02 is set to 1.5 at 16 hours into the simulation); LINK 12 CLOSED AT CLOCKTIME 10 AM LINK 12 OPEN AT CLOCKTIME 8 PM (Two rules: Link 12 is repeatedly closed at 10 am and opened at 8 pm throughout the simulation)

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: controls field
tip: A control is one sentence that opens or closes a link, or gives it a setting, when a water level, a pressure or a time says so.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve copy field
tip: Copies every point as two columns, ready to paste into a spreadsheet.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve equation field
tip: The curve fitted through the given points and used for the pump model.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve note field
tip: What this curve is, in your own words.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve type field
tip: What this curve describes

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curve values field
tip: Select one or two columns in a spreadsheet, copy them, and paste into the first cell you want them to land in. The rows are added as they are needed. You can also paste lines copied straight out of an EPANET file, including the curve name.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: curves field
tip: A curve is a list of points that says how something performs: how much head a pump adds at each flow, how efficient it is at that flow, or how much head a valve loses at each flow.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: fittings field
tip: A fittings list is a set of fittings and their quantities that several pipes can refer to. It adds up to one minor loss coefficient.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: import field
tip: Choose another project file and copy whole libraries from it into this project. Anything whose name is already taken here is skipped and listed, so nothing you already have is changed.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pattern values field
tip: The multipliers, separated by spaces or commas. Paste a column from a spreadsheet if you have one. The list repeats for as long as the run lasts, so it does not have to cover the whole run.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: patterns field
tip: A pattern is a list of multipliers that repeats. Each one applies for one pattern time step, so 24 numbers on a one hour step make a day that repeats. A demand of 10 with a multiplier of 1.5 is 15 at that moment.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pipetype blank field
tip: Blank properties in a pipe type definition are left to be entered individually for each pipe.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pipetypes field
tip: A pipe type is a definition several pipes can refer to for their diameter, roughness and reaction coefficients. Editing the definition edits every pipe that uses it.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: rule field
tip: One clause per line. Descriptions with examples in "ALL CAPS" follow. Line 1: Name of rule, "RULE 1". Line 2: A condition, "IF TANK 2 LEVEL BELOW 17.1". Line 3: An action, "THEN PUMP 9 STATUS IS OPEN". Line 4: A priority, "PRIORITY 1". Add "AND" or "OR" lines to test more than one thing, and "ELSE" lines to say what to do when the test fails. A condition can read LEVEL, HEAD, GRADE, PRESSURE or DEMAND on a node, FLOW, STATUS or SETTING on a link, or TIME and CLOCKTIME on SYSTEM. Use consistent project units. Keywords must be in English.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: rules field
tip: A rule opens or closes a link, or gives it a setting, when a water level, a pressure, a flow or a time reaches a value you set. Rules can test more than one thing at once, and they can say what to do when the test fails.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pipetype detach field
tip: Copies the values this pipe reads from its type into the pipe itself and stops using the type. The pipe’s values don’t change now, and from now on you can edit these values here.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pump curve source field
tip: The curve in the Libraries box that says how much head this pump adds at each flow. Several pumps can use the same curve, and editing it there changes all of them.

where: Libraries box or Properties box curve/type selector: pump effic curve field
tip: The curve in the Libraries box that says how efficient this pump is at each flow. Several pumps can use the same curve, and editing it there changes all of them. This pump holds only the reference; the points themselves are read and edited under Libraries, Curves.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: col static field
tip: The pressure at this junction before any fire flow is drawn, with the system’s ordinary demands still running. Nothing is shut off to measure it, so this is not a zero-flow pressure for the system; it is the same pressure the map shows at this junction. AWWA M31 and NFPA 291 both call this reading the static pressure, and it is where a fire flow test starts.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: design field
tip: A separate question from whether the junction can deliver the flow: with that flow drawn there, does anything else fall below its minimum pressure or exceed its velocity limit? Choosing to check it costs no extra calculation.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: maxvelocity field
tip: A pipe running above this while a fire flow is drawn is reported as a design issue.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: minpressure field
tip: A junction that falls below this while another one is drawing its fire flow is reported as a design issue.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: required node field
tip: The fire flow required at this particular junction for the land use it serves, from your fire code or your fire authority. Leave it blank and the junction is tested against the number in the Fire flow analysis box.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: required field
tip: The flow your fire code or your fire authority requires at a hydrant. Each junction is tested against this number unless it carries a required fire flow of its own.

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: residual field
tip: The pressure the junction must still hold while delivering the fire flow. AWWA M31 and NFPA 291 use 20 psi (140 kPa).

where: Water > Analyze > Fire flow box: scope field
tip: Choose the set before you run. Testing every junction in a large system can take minutes.
Add another demand category at this junction, with its own base demand, pattern and description. The categories add up.
Flows taken out of the network at this node. Enter a negative number for flow put into the network here.
Uncheck this box to leave the asset on the drawing but out of the network: it is drawn grey and the solver ignores it. In a scenario this is how a pipe is switched on and off.
Close this pipe so no water can pass through it. The pipe stays on the map and keeps all its numbers, and you can open it again at any time.
Type a coordinate location to place this node exactly. In a scenario this location applies in that scenario alone, just as dragging it does; in Base it places the node everywhere.
Name or description of this demand category.
How this junction’s demand rises and falls through the run. Leave it at No pattern and the junction follows the project’s Default demand pattern instead.

For your own use, such as a street corner or what a pipe is made of. It is carried into and out of the EPANET file, where it sits at the end of the part's own row. No calculation reads it. A line break becomes a space, because the file has nowhere to put one.
Ground or pipe level at this node. Measure it from any zero you like, as long as every node uses the same one.

An extra outflow that depends on pressure, for a sprinkler, an open outlet, or a modeled leak. The flow it releases is this coefficient times the pressure raised to the emitter exponent, which is set once for the whole network under Settings, Calculation, Hydraulics. Leave it blank on an ordinary junction.
How this reservoir’s water level rises and falls through the run. The head above is multiplied by the pattern.
Water surface level in the reservoir, measured as a height, not as a pressure. Leave it blank to put the water surface at the reservoir elevation.
Loss from the bends, valves, and fittings on this pipe, counted as a multiple of the velocity head. Use 0 for a plain straight pipe.
Length of the pipe. With Auto turned on the length is measured from what you drew. Turn Auto off to type a length that differs from the drawing.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter count field
tip: How many identical services this one customer stands for, so that forty-two single-family connections along one main can be one symbol in one place. The total below is the demand above times this count.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter demand field
tip: What each service at this customer requires. Find and replace can leverage the distinction between blank and 0.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter lumped field
tip: Nearest node; this customer's demands are added there.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter node field
tip: The junction this customer is connected to. Drag the connection point onto a pipe to serve it from a station along that pipe instead.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter offset field
tip: Positive is to the right of the pipe looking from its first node toward its second. Typing a value here can move the customer to the other side of the main, and it always squares the service line to the main.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter pattern field
tip: How this customer’s demand rises and falls through the run. It multiplies the total demand, so it acts on every service this customer stands for. Leave it at No pattern to follow the project’s Default demand pattern.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter pipe field
tip: The asset that this service connects to. Type another one here or in the Customers table to change it, or drag the connection point to a different asset.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter station field
tip: How far along the pipe the service connects, as a percentage of the pipe from its first node to its second. 0 is at one end and 100 is at the other. The circle on the pipe does the same thing with the pointer.

where: Properties box > Customer: meter total field
tip: The demand per service times the number of services. This is the number added to the junction named below.

1 is this pump turning at the speed its curve was measured at. 0.9 is the same pump turning slower, which lowers the head it adds and the flow it passes. A speed pattern takes the place of this number while the run is going.
Hazen-Williams C. A higher number means a smoother pipe: about 150 for new plastic, 130 for new steel or iron, and 100 for old pipe.

How this pump’s speed rises and falls through the run. Each multiplier is the relative speed for that part of the run, and it replaces the Speed setting rather than scaling it, so a multiplier of 0 stops the pump.
A one-word identifier with any meaning you require, such as a pressure zone or a work order.
For a vertical cylinder. Same units as elevation, not pipe diameter. It sets how much water a given depth holds.
Depth of water in the tank, measured up from the tank bottom.
Maximum allowable depth, measured up from the tank bottom.
Minimum allowable depth, measured up from the tank bottom.

where: Properties box: text all zoom field
tip: Keep this text on the drawing however far out you zoom. Untick it and the text hides with the other labels once the view is wider than the labeling threshold set under Map and page.

This text was placed close enough to an asset to follow it, so it moves with that asset and has a leader. A text on a leader takes its horizontal and vertical alignment from the side it sits on, which is why those two rows are not offered while it is attached.
Width of the opening through the valve. The speed of the water through the valve is computed from this width, and the loss follows from that speed.
Loss from the valve body while the valve stands fully open, on top of anything the valve setting removes. It is counted as a multiple of the velocity head. Use 0 to ignore it.

where: Properties box: valve setting drop field
tip: The pressure lost at the valve. A pressure breaker valve always removes exactly this much pressure, whichever way the water is going. It is a drop across the valve, not a pressure to hold.

where: Properties box: valve setting flow field
tip: The most water the valve lets through. When less water than this wants to pass, the valve stands fully open and adds no loss.

where: Properties box: valve setting loss field
tip: How much head the throttle valve removes, counted as a multiple of the velocity head. Use 0 for a valve standing fully open. This one number is the whole of a throttle valve’s loss.

where: Properties box: valve setting pressure field
tip: The pressure the valve keeps. A pressure reducing valve keeps the pressure on its downstream side at or below this value. A pressure sustaining valve keeps the pressure on its upstream side at or above this value.

What the valve does. A throttle valve keeps a fixed loss. The other three keep a pressure or a flow, and open fully, close, or partly close as the water changes. The types control different hydraulic properties, so settings may be lost on change.

where: Properties box > Customer: node customers field
tip: List of customers added at this node (because this was nearest). Customer demands are in addition to other demands listed here. A customer is edited where it sits on the map or in the Customers table.

where: Properties box > Results section: demand field
tip: The flow this node draws at the time step shown: each base demand multiplied by its own pattern, added together. It is calculated, not typed, so it changes with the clock and cannot be edited.

where: Properties box > Results section: gradient field
tip: Head loss divided by the length of the pipe. Use it to compare pipes of different lengths against one design limit.

where: Properties box > Results section: head field
tip: Energy of the water at this node, written as a height of water column. It is an absolute height, where pressure is a gauge measurement.
Elevation of the tank bottom. Water depths in the tank are measured up from here.
Water surface elevation in the tank: the tank bottom elevation plus the water depth.
